chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Natasha had married in the early spring of 1813, and by 1820 already had three daughters, along with a son she had long wished for and was now nursing. She had grown stouter and broader, so that it was hard to recognize, in this robust, motherly woman, the slim, lively Natasha of earlier days. Her features were more defined now, and wore a calm, soft, serene expression. Gone from her face was the ever-glowing animation that used to burn there and had once made up its charm. Now, her face and body were often all that could be seen of her; her soul was not visible at all. All that struck the eye was a strong, handsome, fertile woman. The old fire kindled in her face only very rarely now. It happened only when, as on this particular day, her husband came home, or a sick child was on the mend, or when she and Countess Mary spoke of Prince Andrew—she never mentioned him to her own husband, imagining him to be jealous of Prince Andrew's memory—or, on the rare occasions, something moved her to sing, a habit she had given up almost entirely since her marriage. In those rare moments when the old fire did kindle in her handsome, fully developed body, she was even more striking than she had been in earlier days.

Since their marriage, Natasha and her husband had lived in Moscow, in Petersburg, on their estate near Moscow, or with her mother—that is, in Nicholas's house. Young Countess Bezukhova was not often seen in society, and those who met her there were not pleased with her, and found her neither charming nor amiable. It was not that Natasha disliked solitude—she did not know herself whether she liked it or not, and actually thought she did not—but between her pregnancies, her confinements, the nursing of her children, and sharing every moment of her husband's life, she had demands on her time that could only be met by giving up society altogether. Everyone who had known Natasha before her marriage marveled at the change in her, as at something extraordinary. Only the old countess, with a mother's instinct, had understood that all Natasha's old outbursts had really sprung from her need for children and a husband—as she herself had once cried out at Otradnoe, half in jest but more than half in earnest—and now the countess was surprised by the surprise of those who had never understood Natasha, and kept saying that she had always known Natasha would make an exemplary wife and mother.
"Only she lets her love of her husband and children overflow every bound," the countess would add, "so much so that it becomes almost absurd."

Natasha did not follow the golden rule advocated by clever people, especially the French, which says a girl should not let herself go once she marries, should not neglect her accomplishments, should be even more careful of her appearance than when she was unmarried, and should set out to charm her husband just as much as she did before he became her husband. Natasha, on the contrary, had at once abandoned all her old powers of attraction, of which her singing had been an unusually potent part. She gave it up precisely because it was so powerfully seductive. She took no trouble over her manners, over refinement of speech, over her toilette, or over showing herself to her husband in her most becoming poses, or over sparing him any inconvenience by not being too demanding. She acted against every one of those rules. She felt that the charms her instinct had once taught her to use would now seem simply ridiculous in her husband's eyes—he to whom, from the very first moment, she had given herself entirely, that is, with her whole soul, leaving no corner of it hidden from him. She felt that what bound her to her husband was not the poetic feelings that had once drawn him to her, but something else—indefinite, yet as firm as the bond between her own body and soul.

To fluff up her curls, put on fashionable dresses, and sing romantic songs in order to charm her husband would have struck her as strange as adorning herself to attract herself. Adorning herself for other people might, perhaps, have been agreeable—she did not know—but she simply had no time at all for it. The chief reason she gave no time to singing, or to dress, or to choosing her words carefully, was that she truly had no time to spare for such things.

We know that a person has the capacity to become completely absorbed in a subject, however trivial it might be, and that there is no subject so trivial that it will not swell to infinite proportions if one's whole attention is fixed on it.

The subject that wholly absorbed Natasha's attention was her family: that is, her husband, whom she had to hold onto so that he would belong entirely to her and to the home, and the children, whom she had to bear, bring into the world, nurse, and raise.

And the more deeply she penetrated into the subject that absorbed her—not with her mind alone, but with her whole soul, her whole being—the larger that subject grew, and the weaker and more inadequate her own powers appeared to her, so that she poured them wholly into that one thing and still could not accomplish everything she believed was needed.

There were, then as now, conversations and arguments about women's rights, about the relations of husband and wife and their freedom and their rights, though these subjects were not yet called "questions" the way they are now; but these topics were not merely uninteresting to Natasha—she simply did not understand them at all.

These questions, then as now, exist only for people who see nothing in marriage but the pleasure married people get from one another—that is, only the beginning of marriage, and not its full meaning, which lies in the family.

Discussions and questions of that kind—rather like the question of how to get the most enjoyment out of one's dinner—did not exist then, and do not exist now, for people whose purpose in eating dinner is the nourishment it provides, just as the purpose of marriage is the family.

If the purpose of dinner is to nourish the body, a man who eats two dinners at once may perhaps enjoy himself more, but he will not achieve his purpose, since his stomach will not be able to digest two dinners.
If the purpose of marriage is the family, then a person who wants many wives or many husbands may perhaps get a great deal of pleasure out of it, but in that case will not have a family.

If the purpose of food is nourishment, and the purpose of marriage is the family, then the whole question comes down to this: not eating more than one can digest, and not having more wives or husbands than are needed for a family—that is, one wife, or one husband. Natasha needed a husband. A husband was given her, and he gave her a family. And not only did she see no need for any other or better husband, but since every power of her soul was bent on serving that husband and that family, she could not imagine, and saw no point in imagining, how things might be if they were different.

Natasha did not care for society in general, but she prized all the more the company of her relatives—Countess Mary, her brother, her mother, and Sonya. She valued the company of those she could come striding to, disheveled, straight from the nursery, still in her dressing gown, to show off, with a joyful face, a yellow stain instead of a green one on the baby's diaper, and from whom she could hear the reassuring words that the baby was much better.

Natasha had let herself go to such an extent that the way she dressed and did her hair, her careless choice of words, and her jealousy—she was jealous of Sonya, of the governess, of every woman, pretty or plain—had become the standing joke of everyone around her. The general opinion was that Pierre was under his wife's thumb, which was in fact perfectly true. From the very first days of their marriage Natasha had made her demands plain. Pierre was greatly surprised by his wife's view—entirely new to him—that every moment of his life belonged to her and to the family. His wife's demands astonished him, but they flattered him too, and he submitted to them.

Pierre's subjection showed itself in the fact that he did not dare so much as flirt with another woman, or even speak to one with a smile; did not dare dine at the club just for amusement; did not dare spend money on a whim; and did not dare stay away for any length of time except on business—under which his wife included his intellectual pursuits, which she did not understand in the least, but to which she attached the greatest importance. To make up for all this, at home Pierre had the right to arrange his own life and that of the whole family exactly as he pleased. At home Natasha placed herself in the position of a slave to her husband, and the whole household walked on tiptoe whenever he was occupied—that is, reading or writing in his study. Pierre had only to show a fondness for something to have it done for him every time, without fail. He had only to express a wish, and Natasha would jump up and run to fulfill it.

The entire household was run according to Pierre's supposed wishes—that is, according to what Natasha guessed his wishes to be. Where and how they lived, their acquaintances and connections, Natasha's own occupations, the children's upbringing—all of it was chosen not merely with an eye to Pierre's stated wishes, but to what Natasha, judging from thoughts he had expressed in conversation, supposed his wishes to be. And she read his real wishes quite correctly, and having once arrived at them, held to them tenaciously. When Pierre himself wanted to change his mind, she would fight him with his own weapons.

So, for instance, in a time of trouble that stayed forever memorable to him, after the birth of their first, delicate child, when they had to change wet nurses three times and Natasha fell ill from despair, Pierre had once told her of Rousseau's view, with which he entirely agreed, that having a wet nurse is unnatural and harmful. When their next baby was born, despite the opposition of her mother, the doctors, and even her own husband—all of whom were strongly against her nursing the baby herself, a thing then unheard of and considered harmful—she insisted on having her own way, and after that nursed every one of her babies herself.

It very often happened that, in a moment's irritation, husband and wife would fall into a dispute, but long afterward Pierre, to his surprise and delight, would find in his wife's ideas and actions the very thought she had argued against, but stripped now of everything superfluous that, in the heat of the dispute, he had piled onto it while stating his own opinion.

After seven years of marriage, Pierre had the joyful, settled certainty that he was not a bad man, and he felt this because he saw himself reflected in his wife. He felt the good and the bad within himself tangled and overlapping. But only what was truly good in him was reflected back in his wife; everything not quite good was cast aside. And this was not the result of any reasoning on her part—it was a direct and mysterious reflection.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Two months before, while Pierre was already staying with the Rostovs, he had received a letter from Prince Theodore, asking him to come to Petersburg to confer on some important questions then being discussed by a society of which Pierre was one of the principal founders.

On reading that letter—she always read her husband's letters—Natasha herself suggested that he go to Petersburg, though his absence would be a real hardship for her. She attached tremendous importance to all her husband's intellectual and abstract concerns, though she did not understand them, and she always dreaded being any hindrance to him in such matters. To Pierre's timid, questioning look after reading the letter she answered by urging him to go, but insisting he fix a definite date for his return. He was given four weeks' leave.
Ever since that leave had run out, more than two weeks before, Natasha had been in a constant state of alarm, low spirits, and irritability.

Denisov, now a retired general and thoroughly dissatisfied with the current state of affairs, had arrived during that fortnight. He looked at Natasha with sorrow and astonishment, as at a poor likeness of someone once dear to him. A dull, dejected look, distracted answers, and talk about the nursery were all he saw and heard from the woman who had once enchanted him.

Natasha was low-spirited and irritable the whole time, most of all when her mother, her brother, Sonya, or Countess Mary, trying to console her, attempted to excuse Pierre and suggest reasons for the delay in his return.

"It's all nonsense, all rubbish—those endless discussions that lead nowhere, and all those idiotic societies!" Natasha would say of the very affairs whose immense importance she herself firmly believed in.

And she would go off to the nursery to nurse Petya, her only boy. Nothing and no one could tell her anything so comforting or so reasonable as this little three-month-old creature, when he lay at her breast and she felt the movement of his lips and the snuffling of his tiny nose. That little creature seemed to say: "You're angry, you're jealous, you'd like to make him pay for it, you're afraid—but here I am! And I am him..." and there was no answering that. It was more than true.

During that anxious fortnight Natasha turned to the baby for comfort so often, and fussed over him so much, that she overfed him, and he fell ill. She was terrified by his illness—and yet that was exactly what she needed. Taken up with worrying over him, she bore her worry about her husband more easily.

She was nursing her boy when the sound of Pierre's sleigh was heard at the front door, and the old nurse—who knew how to please her mistress—came into the room inaudibly, but in a hurry, her face beaming.
"Has he come?" Natasha asked quickly, in a whisper, afraid to move for fear of waking the dozing baby.
"He's come, ma'am," whispered the nurse.

The blood rushed to Natasha's face, and her feet moved of their own accord, but she could not jump up and run out. The baby opened his eyes again and looked at her. "You're here?" he seemed to be saying, and lazily smacked his lips once more.

Carefully drawing her breast away, Natasha rocked him a little, handed him to the nurse, and went toward the door with quick steps. But at the door she stopped, as if her conscience reproached her for abandoning the child so soon in her joy, and she looked back. The nurse, elbows raised, was lifting the baby over the rail of his cot.
"Go on, ma'am! Don't you worry, go!" she whispered, smiling, with the kind of easy familiarity that grows up between a nurse and her mistress.
Natasha ran with quick, light footsteps to the anteroom.
Denisov, who had come out of the study into the dance room with his pipe, now, for the first time, recognized the old Natasha. A flood of bright, joyful light poured from her transfigured face.
"He's come!" she cried as she ran past, and Denisov found that he too was delighted that Pierre, whom he did not much care for, had come home.

Reaching the vestibule, Natasha saw a tall figure in a fur coat unwinding his scarf. "It's him! It's really him! He's come!" she told herself, and, rushing at him, threw her arms around him, pressed his head to her chest, then pushed him back and gazed at his ruddy, happy face, covered in hoarfrost. "Yes, it's him, happy and contented...."

Then all at once she remembered the torment of suspense she had suffered for the last two weeks, and the joy lighting up her face vanished; she frowned and let loose on Pierre a torrent of reproaches and angry words.

"Yes, it's all very well for you. You're pleased, you've had a wonderful time.... But what about me? You might at least have thought of the children. I'm nursing, and my milk went bad.... Petya was at death's door. But you were off enjoying yourself. Yes, enjoying yourself..."

Pierre knew he was not to blame, since he could not have come any sooner; he knew this outburst was unreasonable and would blow over in a minute or two; above all, he knew he himself was cheerful and happy. He wanted to smile, but did not dare even think of it. He made a piteous, frightened face and bowed his head.
"I couldn't help it, on my honor. But how's Petya?"
"He's fine now. Come along! You ought to be ashamed of yourself! If only you could see what I was like without you, how I suffered!"
"You're well?"
"Come, come!" she said, not letting go of his arm. And they went off to their rooms.

When Nicholas and his wife came looking for Pierre, he was in the nursery, holding his baby son, who had woken up again, on his huge right palm, dandling him. A blissful, radiant smile was fixed on the baby's broad face, its mouth open, toothless. The storm had long since passed, and bright, joyful sunshine lit Natasha's face as she gazed tenderly at her husband and child.
"And did you talk everything over well with Prince Theodore?" she asked.
"Yes, splendidly."
"You see, he holds it up." She meant the baby's head. "But how he frightened me... Have you seen the princess? Is it true she's in love with that..."
"Yes, just imagine..."

At that moment Nicholas and Countess Mary came in. Pierre, still holding the baby, bent down, kissed them, and answered their questions. But despite all the interesting things there were to discuss, the baby, in his little cap perched on his unsteady head, plainly held all of Pierre's attention.

"How sweet!" said Countess Mary, looking at and playing with the baby. "Now, Nicholas," she added, turning to her husband, "I simply can't understand how you don't see the charm of these darling little marvels."
"I don't, and I can't," replied Nicholas, looking coldly at the baby. "A lump of flesh. Come along, Pierre!"
"And yet he's such an affectionate father," said Countess Mary, defending her husband, "only once they're a year old or so..."
"Pierre nurses them wonderfully now," said Natasha. "He says his hand was made just for a baby to sit in. Just look!"
"Only not for this..." Pierre suddenly burst out laughing, and, shifting the baby, handed him to the nurse.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 12
paragraphs: As in every large household, at Bald Hills there existed several quite distinct worlds, which merged into one harmonious whole, though each kept its own particular character and made concessions to the others. Every event that took place in that house, joyful or sad, mattered to all these worlds, but each had its own particular reasons for rejoicing or grieving over it, independent of the others.
Pierre's return, for instance, was a joyful and important event, and every one of them felt it to be so.

The servants—the most reliable judges of their masters, since they judge not by what they say or the feelings they express but by their actions and their way of living—were glad of Pierre's return, because they knew that with him around Count Nicholas would stop going out to the estate every single day, and would be in better spirits and a better temper, and also because they would all get handsome presents at the holidays.

The children and their governesses were glad of Pierre's return because no one else drew them into the social life of the household the way he did. He alone could play, on the clavichord, that écossaise—his only piece—to which, as he said, every possible kind of dance could be danced, and they felt certain he had brought presents for every one of them.

Young Nicholas, now a slim, delicate boy of fifteen with intelligent eyes and curly light-brown hair, was thrilled, because Uncle Pierre, as he called him, was the object of his rapturous, passionate devotion. No one had planted this love of Pierre in him; he saw him only now and then. Countess Mary, who had raised him, had done everything she could to make him love her husband the way she loved him, and little Nicholas did love his uncle, but with just a shade of contempt mixed in. Pierre, though, he adored. He did not want to be a hussar or a Knight of St. George like Uncle Nicholas; he wanted to be learned, and wise, and kind, like Pierre. In Pierre's presence his face always lit up with pleasure, and he would flush and go breathless whenever Pierre spoke to him. He never missed a single word Pierre said, and would afterward, with Dessalles or alone, recall and turn over in his mind the meaning of everything Pierre had said. Pierre's past life, and his unhappiness before 1812—of which young Nicholas had formed a vague, poetic picture from a few words he had overheard—his adventures in Moscow, his captivity, Platon Karataev, of whom he had heard from Pierre, his love for Natasha, of whom the boy was also especially fond, and above all Pierre's friendship with the father Nicholas could not remember—all of it made Pierre, in his eyes, a hero and a saint.

From scraps overheard about Natasha and his father, from the emotion with which Pierre spoke of that dead father, and from the careful, reverent tenderness with which Natasha spoke of him, the boy, only just beginning to guess what love was, had formed the idea that his father had loved Natasha, and, dying, had left her to his friend. But the father the boy could not remember appeared to him as a kind of divinity he could not picture, one he never thought of without his heart swelling and tears of sadness and rapture coming to his eyes. And so the boy, too, was happy that Pierre had arrived.
The guests welcomed Pierre because he always helped enliven and bring together whatever company he found himself in.
The grown members of the family, not to mention his wife, were glad to have back a friend whose presence made life run more smoothly and peacefully.
The old ladies were pleased with the presents he brought them, and, above all, that Natasha would now go back to being herself.
Pierre sensed the different expectations of all these different worlds, and hurried to satisfy them all.

Absent-minded and forgetful as he was, the most absent-minded and forgetful of men, Pierre, with the help of a list his wife had drawn up, had now bought everything—not forgetting his mother- and brother-in-law's commissions, nor the dress material meant as a present for Belova, nor the toys for his wife's nephews. In the early days of their marriage it had struck him as strange that his wife should expect him not to forget to buy every single thing he had undertaken to buy, and he had been taken aback by her real annoyance the first time he came home from a trip having forgotten everything. But in time he grew used to this expectation. Knowing that Natasha never asked anything for herself, and only gave him commissions for others when he himself had first offered to take them on, he now found an unexpected, almost childlike pleasure in buying presents for everyone in the house, and never forgot a single one. If Natasha found fault with him now, it was only for buying too much, and things that were too expensive. To her other supposed faults—untidiness and neglect of her own appearance, faults most people saw as such but which Pierre thought of as qualities—she had now added stinginess.

From the time Pierre began living as a family man, on a footing that meant heavy expenses, he had noticed, to his surprise, that he spent only half what he used to, and that his affairs—which had been in disorder lately, chiefly because of his first wife's debts—had begun to improve.

Life had become cheaper because it was more confined: that most expensive luxury of all, the kind of life that can be changed at any moment, was no longer his, and he no longer wanted it. He felt that his way of life had now been settled once and for all, until death, and that it was no longer in his power to change it, and so, in that sense, his way of life had turned out to be economical.
With a merry, smiling face, Pierre was sorting through his purchases.
"What do you think of this?" he said, unrolling a piece of cloth like a shopkeeper.
Natasha, sitting across from him with her eldest daughter on her lap, turned her sparkling eyes swiftly from her husband to the things he was showing her.
"That's for Belova? Excellent!" She felt the quality of the material. "A ruble an arshin, I suppose?"
Pierre told her the price.

"Too dear!" Natasha said. "How pleased the children will be, and Mamma too! Only you needn't have bought me this," she added, unable to hold back a smile as she gazed admiringly at a gold comb set with pearls, of a kind just then coming into fashion.
"Adele tempted me: she kept insisting I buy it," Pierre answered.
"When am I supposed to wear it?" and Natasha stuck it into her coil of hair. "When I take little Masha into society? Maybe it'll be fashionable again by then. Well, come along now."
And, gathering up the presents, they went first to the nursery, and then to the old countess's rooms.
The countess was sitting with her companion Belova, playing a game of grand-patience as usual, when Pierre and Natasha came into the drawing room with parcels under their arms.
The countess was now past sixty, entirely gray, and wore a cap with a frill framing her face. Her face had shriveled, her upper lip had sunk in, and her eyes had grown dim.

After the deaths of her son and her husband in such quick succession, she felt herself a person accidentally forgotten by the world, left with no aim or purpose for her existence. She ate, drank, slept, or lay awake, but she did not live. Life gave her no new impressions. She wanted nothing from life but peace, and only death could give her that peace. But until death came she had to go on living—that is, to keep using her vital forces. A peculiarity one notices in very small children and very old people alike was especially plain in her. Her life had no outward aims left—only a need to keep exercising her various functions and inclinations remained visible. She had to eat, sleep, think, speak, weep, work, vent her anger, and so on, simply because she had a stomach, a brain, muscles, nerves, and a liver. She did none of these things under any outward pressure, the way people in the full vigor of life do, for whom the purpose behind exercising their own functions goes unnoticed, hidden behind whatever goal they're chasing. She talked only because she had a physical need to exercise her tongue and lungs. She cried the way a child cries, because her nose needed clearing, and so on. What is a goal, for people in full vigor, was for her plainly nothing but a pretext.
So, in the mornings—especially if she had eaten something rich the day before—she would feel a need to be angry, and would seize on the handiest pretext: Belova's deafness.
She would begin saying something to her, in a low voice, from the far end of the room.
"It seems a little warmer today, my dear," she would murmur.
And when Belova answered, "Oh yes, they've come," she would mutter angrily: "Good Lord! How stupid and deaf she is!"

Another pretext would be her snuff, which would seem too dry, or too damp, or not ground fine enough. After these fits of irritation her face would turn yellow, and her maids knew, by unfailing signs, exactly when Belova would be deaf again, the snuff damp again, and the countess's face yellow again. Just as she needed to work off her ill temper, so too she sometimes needed to exercise her still-surviving faculty of thought—and the pretext for that was a game of patience. When she needed to cry, the late count would serve as pretext. When she wanted to be agitated, Nicholas and his health would be the pretext, and when she felt the need to speak spitefully, Countess Mary would serve. When her vocal organs needed exercise, usually around seven o'clock, once she had rested after dinner in a darkened room, the pretext would be retelling the same old stories over and over to the same listeners.

The old lady's condition was understood by the whole household, though no one ever spoke of it aloud, and everyone made every possible effort to see to her needs. Only in a rare glance, exchanged with a sad smile between Nicholas, Pierre, Natasha, and Countess Mary, was their shared understanding of her condition ever expressed.

But those glances said something more besides: they said that she had already played her part in life, that what they now saw before them was not the whole of her, that all of them must one day become like her, and that they were glad to give way to her, to hold themselves back for the sake of this once-precious person, once as full of life as they themselves now were, but now so much to be pitied. "Memento mori," said those glances.
Only the truly heartless, the stupid ones in that household, and the very young children failed to understand this, and steered clear of her.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: When Pierre and his wife came into the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual moods, the kind that needed the mental effort of a game of patience, and so—though out of sheer habit she greeted him with the words she always used whenever Pierre or her son came back after an absence: "High time, my dear, high time! We were all tired of waiting for you. Well, thank God!" and received her presents with another of her customary remarks: "It's not the gift that matters, my dear, but that you gave it to me, an old woman..."—still, it was plain she was not really pleased at Pierre's arrival just then, since it drew her attention away from the unfinished game.

She finished her game of patience before she even examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sèvres teacup painted with shepherdesses and fitted with a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the count's portrait on the lid, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had long wanted a box of just that kind, but, not wanting to cry just then, she glanced indifferently at the portrait and gave her chief attention to the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all, you've brought yourself back—I never saw anything like it, you really ought to give your wife a scolding! What are we to do with her? She's like a madwoman when you're away. Doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she went on, repeating her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeyevna," she added, turning to her companion, "see what a card box my son has brought us!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had a great deal to talk over that they could not discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind in so many things that if they had started talking in her presence, they would have had to answer questions that made no sense anymore, and repeat things they had already told her many times over: that so-and-so was dead, that so-and-so had married, all of which she would once again be unable to remember—still, out of habit, they all sat down to tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the countess's questions about whether Prince Vasili had aged, and whether Countess Mary Alexeyevna sent her greetings and still thought of them, and other matters that interested no one, including the countess herself.

This kind of conversation, interesting to no one and yet unavoidable, went on all through teatime. All the grown members of the family had gathered around the round tea table, where Sonya presided over the samovar. The children, with their tutors and governesses, had already had their tea, and their voices could be heard from the next room. At tea, everyone sat in their accustomed places: Nicholas by the stove, at a small table where his tea was brought to him; Milka, the old gray borzoi bitch, daughter of the first Milka, her face now quite gray and her large black eyes seeming more prominent than ever, lay in the armchair beside him; Denisov, his curly hair, mustache, and whiskers now half gray, sat beside Countess Mary, his general's tunic unbuttoned; Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He talked about the things he knew would interest the old lady and that she could follow. He told her of goings-on in society, and about the people who had once made up the circle of her contemporaries, a real, living, distinct group, but who were now for the most part scattered about the world, and, like herself, were gathering in the last ears of the harvests they had sown in earlier years. But to the old countess, those contemporaries of hers still seemed the only serious, real society there was. Natasha could tell, from how animated Pierre was, that his visit had been eventful and that he had a great deal to tell them, but did not dare say it in front of the old countess. Denisov, not being a member of the family, did not grasp Pierre's caution, and, being a malcontent deeply interested in what was going on in Petersburg, kept pressing Pierre to tell them what was happening in the Semyonovsky regiment, then about Arakcheev, then about the Bible Society. Once or twice Pierre got carried away and began speaking of these things, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan and Countess Mary Alexeyevna.
"Well, and all this idiocy—Gossner and Tatáwinova? Is that weally still going on?" Denisov asked.
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Why, more than ever! The Bible Society is running the whole government now!"

"What's that, mon cher ami?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and plainly needed a pretext for being angry now that her meal was done. "What's this about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Maman," Nicholas put in, knowing just how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has great influence, they say."
"Arakcheev and Golitsyn," Pierre put in, without thinking, "are the whole government now! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are afraid of everything."

"Well, and how is Prince Alexander to blame? He's a most estimable man. I used to meet him at Mary Antonovna's," the countess said, in an offended tone; and, still more offended that everyone had fallen silent, she went on: "These days everyone finds fault with everything. A Gospel Society! Well, and what's the harm in that?" and she rose—everyone else got up too—and, with a stern expression, sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The melancholy silence that followed was broken by the sound of the children's voices and laughter from the next room. Some jolly commotion was plainly going on there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shriek rose above the rest.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas—he never once lost sight of Natasha—and smiled happily.
"That's delightful music!" he said.
"It means Anna Makarovna has finished her stocking," said Countess Mary.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. When I was driving here today, the closer I got to the house, the more anxious I grew. As soon as I stepped into the anteroom, I heard Andrusha's peals of laughter, and I knew right then that everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I mustn't go in there—those stockings are supposed to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went off to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew louder still.

"Come, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here, into the middle of the room, and at the word of command, 'One, two'—and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and a silence fell: "three!"—and a rapturous, breathless shout of children's voices filled the room. "Two, two!" they shouted.

This meant two stockings, which, by some secret method known only to herself, Anna Makarovna would knit at the same time on the same needles, and which, once they were finished, she would always draw out triumphantly, one from inside the other, right in front of the children.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: Soon after this the children came in to say good night. They kissed everyone, the tutors and governesses made their bows, and they went out. Only young Nicholas and his tutor stayed behind. Dessalles whispered to the boy to come downstairs.
"No, Monsieur Dessalles, I'll ask my aunt to let me stay," answered Nicholas Bolkonsky, also in a whisper.
"Ma tante, please let me stay," he said, going up to his aunt.
His face was full of entreaty, agitation, and ecstasy. Countess Mary glanced at him and turned to Pierre.
"When you're here, he can't tear himself away," she said.

"I'll bring him to you directly, Monsieur Dessalles. Good night!" said Pierre, offering his hand to the Swiss tutor, and then he turned to young Nicholas with a smile. "You and I haven't had a proper look at each other yet.... How he's grown to look like him, Mary!" he added, turning to Countess Mary.
"Like my father?" the boy asked, flushing crimson, looking up at Pierre with bright, rapturous eyes.

Pierre nodded, and went on with what he had been saying before the children interrupted. Countess Mary sat down to her woolwork; Natasha never took her eyes off her husband. Nicholas and Denisov got up, asked for their pipes, smoked, went to fetch more tea from Sonya, who sat weary but resolute at the samovar, and put questions to Pierre. The curly-headed, delicate boy sat unnoticed in a corner, his eyes shining, starting every now and then and muttering something under his breath, clearly caught up in some new and powerful feeling as he kept turning his curly head, with its thin neck bared by his turned-down collar, toward the place where Pierre sat.

The conversation turned to the current gossip about those in power—the subject most people find of greatest interest in domestic politics. Denisov, dissatisfied with the government on account of his own disappointments in the service, listened with pleasure to the things being done in Petersburg, things that struck him as foolish, and made sharp, forceful remarks on everything Pierre told them.

"One used to have to be German—now one has to dance attendance on Tatáwinova and Madame Kwüdener, and wead Ecka'tshausen and the bwethwen. Oh, they should just turn that fine fellow Bonaparte loose again—he'd knock all this nonsense out of them! Fancy giving command of the Semyonov wegiment to a fellow like that Schwa'tz!" he cried.

Nicholas, though he lacked Denisov's readiness to find fault with everything, also thought that discussing the government was a very serious, weighty matter, and it seemed to him a matter of real importance that A had been appointed Minister of This, and B Governor General of That, and that the Emperor had said such and such, and this minister had said such and such. And so he thought it his duty to take an interest in these things, and questioned Pierre closely. The questions the two of them put kept the conversation from straying beyond its ordinary character—gossip about the upper reaches of government.

But Natasha, who knew all her husband's ways and ideas, could see that he had long been wanting, without managing it, to steer the conversation onto another track and give voice to the idea he felt so deeply, the very idea for whose sake he had gone to Petersburg to consult with his new friend Prince Theodore, and she came to his aid by asking how things had gone with Prince Theodore.
"What was it about?" asked Nicholas.

"Always the same thing," said Pierre, glancing around at his listeners. "Everyone can see things have gotten so bad that they can't go on this way any longer, and that it's the duty of every decent man to work against it as far as he can."
"What can decent men do?" Nicholas asked, frowning slightly. "What is there to be done?"
"Well, this..."
"Come into my study," said Nicholas.

Natasha, who had long expected to be sent for to nurse her baby, now heard the nurse calling her and went off to the nursery. Countess Mary followed her. The men went into the study, and little Nicholas Bolkonsky, unnoticed by his uncle, followed them in and sat down at the writing table, in a shadowy corner by the window.
"Well, what would you do?" asked Denisov.
"Always some fantastic scheme or other," said Nicholas.

"Why this," Pierre began, not sitting down but pacing the room, sometimes stopping short, gesturing, and lisping: "the situation in Petersburg is this. The Emperor pays no attention to anything anymore. He's given himself over entirely to this mysticism"—Pierre could no longer stand mysticism in anyone—"he only wants peace, and only these people, sans foi ni loi,* can give it to him—people who go around recklessly hacking and strangling everything: Magnitsky, Arakcheev, and the rest of that crowd.... You'll agree that if you didn't oversee your own estates yourself, and only wanted a quiet life, the harsher your steward was, the more easily your object would be achieved," he said to Nicholas.
* Without faith or law.
"Well, and where does that lead?" said Nicholas.

"Well, everything is going to ruin! Robbery in the law courts, nothing in the army but flogging, drilling, and Military Settlements; the people are being tormented, education is being crushed. Everything young and honest is being ground down! Everyone can see this can't go on. Everything is stretched so tight that it's bound to snap," said Pierre—much as everyone who has ever examined the actions of any government has said, since governments began. "I told them just one thing, in Petersburg."
"Told whom?"

"Well, you know whom," said Pierre, with a meaningful glance from under his brows. "Prince Theodore and the rest of them. Encouraging culture and philanthropy is all very well, of course. The aim is excellent—but under the present circumstances, something else is needed."
At that moment Nicholas noticed his nephew was in the room. His face darkened, and he went up to the boy.
"Why are you in here?"

"Why? Let him stay," said Pierre, taking Nicholas by the arm and going on. "That's not enough, I told them. Something else is needed. When you're standing there expecting the overstretched string to snap at any moment, when everyone is expecting the inevitable catastrophe, then as many people as possible need to join hands, as tightly as they can, to stand against the coming disaster. Everything young and strong is being lured away and corrupted. One man is drawn off by women, another by honors, a third by ambition or money, and off they go, over to that camp. There are no independent men left—men like you or me. What I'm saying is: widen the scope of our society, let the watchword be not virtue alone, but independence and action as well!"
Nicholas, who had let go of his nephew, irritably pulled up an armchair, sat down in it, and listened to Pierre, coughing with displeasure and frowning more and more.
"But action toward what end?" he burst out. "And what position would you take toward the government?"

"Why, the position of helpers. The society needn't be secret at all, if the government allows it. It's not just not hostile to the government—it's a society of true conservatives, a society of gentlemen in the fullest sense of the word. Its whole purpose is to stop some Pugachev or other from murdering my children and yours, and to stop Arakcheev from sending me off to some Military Settlement. We join hands only for the public good and the general safety."
"Yes, but it's a secret society, and so a hostile one, a harmful one, one that can only do harm."

"Why? Did the Tugendbund, which saved Europe"—they did not yet dare suggest that it was Russia that had saved Europe—"do any harm? The Tugendbund is an alliance of virtue: it's love, mutual aid... it's what Christ preached on the Cross."

Natasha, who had come in during the conversation, looked happily at her husband. It was not what he was saying that pleased her—that did not even interest her, since to her it all seemed extremely simple, and she felt she had known it for a long time, because she knew it sprang from Pierre's whole soul—but it was his animated, enthusiastic look that made her glad.

The boy with the thin neck rising from his turned-down collar—whom everyone had forgotten about—watched Pierre with even greater and more rapturous delight. Every word Pierre spoke burned itself into his heart, and, with a nervous movement of his fingers, he found himself unconsciously breaking the sealing wax and the quill pens that came to hand on his uncle's table.
"It isn't at all what you think; but that's what the German Tugendbund was, and it's what I'm proposing."

"No, my fwiend! The Tugendbund's all vewy well for sausage eaters, but I don't understand it and can't even pwonounce it," Denisov broke in, loudly and firmly. "I agwee that evewything here is wotten and howwible, but the Tugendbund I don't understand. If we're not satisfied, let's have a wevolt of our own. That's fine by me. Je suis vot'e homme!"*
* "I'm your man."

Pierre smiled, Natasha burst out laughing, but Nicholas only knitted his brows further, and set about proving to Pierre that there was no real prospect of any great change, and that all the danger Pierre spoke of existed only in his own imagination. Pierre argued the opposite, and, since his mental powers were greater and more resourceful, Nicholas found himself cornered. This only made him angrier still, since he was fully convinced—not by reasoning, but by something inside him stronger than reason—of the rightness of his own view.

"I'll tell you this," he said, standing up and trying, with nervously twitching fingers, to prop his pipe up in a corner, then finally giving up the attempt. "I can't prove it to you. You say everything here is rotten, and that a collapse is coming: I don't see it. But you also say our oath of allegiance is some kind of conditional thing, and to that I say: 'You are my best friend, as you well know, but if you formed a secret society and started working against the government—whatever government it may be—I know it's my duty to obey the government. And if Arakcheev ordered me to lead a squadron against you and cut you down, I wouldn't hesitate an instant, and I'd do it.' Argue about that all you like!"

An awkward silence followed these words. Natasha was the first to speak, defending her husband and attacking her brother. Her defense was weak and clumsy, but it did what she wanted. The conversation started up again, no longer in the unpleasantly hostile tone of Nicholas's last words.
When they all got up to go in to supper, little Nicholas Bolkonsky went up to Pierre, pale, his eyes shining and radiant.
"Uncle Pierre, you... no... If Papa were alive... would he agree with you?" he asked.

And Pierre suddenly grasped what a special, independent, complicated, and powerful process of thought and feeling must have been going on in this boy throughout the whole conversation, and, remembering everything he had said, he wished the lad had not heard him. Still, he had to give him some answer.
"Yes, I think so," he said, reluctantly, and left the study.
The boy looked down and seemed only now to notice what he had done to the things on the table. He flushed and went up to Nicholas.
"Uncle, forgive me, I did that... without meaning to," he said, pointing to the broken sealing wax and pens.
Nicholas started angrily.
"All right, all right," he said, throwing the bits under the table.
And, plainly holding back his irritation with some effort, he turned away from the boy.
"You shouldn't have been in here at all," he said.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: The talk at supper was not about politics or secret societies, but turned to the subject Nicholas liked best of all—memories of 1812. Denisov set it going, and Pierre was particularly agreeable and amusing on the subject. The family parted for the night on the friendliest terms.

After supper Nicholas, having undressed in his study and given his instructions to the steward, who had been waiting for him, went to the bedroom in his dressing gown, where he found his wife still at her table, writing.
"What are you writing, Mary?" Nicholas asked.
Countess Mary blushed. She was afraid that what she was writing would not be understood or approved of by her husband.
She had wanted to keep what she was writing hidden from him, but at the same time she was glad he had caught her at it, glad that she would now have to tell him.
"A diary, Nicholas," she answered, handing him a blue exercise book filled with her firm, bold handwriting.
"A diary?" Nicholas repeated, with a touch of irony, and picked up the book.
It was written in French.

December 4. Today when Andrusha (her eldest boy) woke up, he did not want to dress, and Mademoiselle Louise sent for me. He was naughty and stubborn. I tried threats, but that only made him angrier. So I took the matter in hand: I left him alone and, with nurse's help, began getting the other children up, telling him I did not love him. For a long time he was silent, as if astonished, then he jumped out of bed, ran to me in his shirt, and sobbed so hard that I could not calm him for a long time. It was plain that what troubled him most was that he had grieved me. Later, in the evening, when I gave him his ticket, he again began to cry piteously and kiss me. One can get him to do anything through tenderness.
"What's a 'ticket'?" Nicholas asked.
"I've started giving the older ones marks every evening, showing how they've behaved."

Nicholas looked into the radiant eyes gazing up at him, and went on turning the pages and reading. In the diary, everything in the children's lives that had struck their mother as worth noting, whether as a sign of their character or as the basis for some general reflection on methods of upbringing, had been set down. Most of it was insignificant trifles, but they did not seem so either to the mother or, now, reading this diary about his own children for the first time, to the father.
Under the date "5" was entered:

Mitya was naughty at table. Papa said he was to have no pudding. He had none, but he looked so unhappily and greedily at the others while they were eating! I think that punishing children by depriving them of sweets only makes them greedier. Must tell Nicholas this.

Nicholas set the book down and looked at his wife. The radiant eyes gazed back at him questioningly: would he approve of her diary, or disapprove? There could be no doubt of his approval—or of his admiration for his wife.

Perhaps it needn't be done quite so pedantically, Nicholas thought, or even be done at all, but this tireless, unceasing spiritual effort, whose only aim was the children's moral welfare, delighted him. Had Nicholas been able to put his feelings into words, he would have found that his steady, tender, proud love for his wife rested on his sense of wonder at her spiritual depth, and at the lofty moral world, almost beyond his own reach, in which she had her being.

He was proud of her intelligence and her goodness, recognized his own insignificance beside her in that spiritual world, and rejoiced all the more that a soul like hers not only belonged to him, but was part of himself.

"I quite, quite approve, my dearest!" he said, with a meaningful look, and, after a short pause, added: "And I behaved badly today. You weren't in the study. We got into an argument—Pierre and I—and I lost my temper. But he's impossible: such a child! I don't know what would become of him if Natasha didn't keep him in hand.... Do you have any idea why he went to Petersburg? They've formed..."
"Yes, I know," said Countess Mary. "Natasha told me."

"Well then, you know," Nicholas went on, growing hot all over again just remembering their discussion, "he wanted to convince me it's every honest man's duty to go against the government, and that the oath of allegiance and one's duty... I'm sorry you weren't there. They all fell on me—Denisov and Natasha... Natasha is absurd. The way she rules over him! And yet the moment there's an actual argument, she has no words of her own, only repeats his," added Nicholas, giving in to that irresistible urge that tempts us to sit in judgment over the people closest and dearest to us. He forgot that what he was saying about Natasha could be applied, word for word, to himself, in relation to his own wife.
"Yes, I've noticed that," said Countess Mary.
"When I told him that duty and the oath stand above everything, he set about proving I don't know what! A pity you weren't there—what would you have said?"

"As I see it, you were quite right, and I told Natasha so. Pierre says everyone is suffering, being tormented and corrupted, and that it's our duty to help our neighbor. Of course he's right about that," said Countess Mary, "but he forgets that we have other duties closer to home, duties God Himself has laid on us, and that though we might risk ourselves, we mustn't risk our children."

"Yes, that's it exactly! That's just what I told him," put in Nicholas, who fancied he really had said it. "But they kept insisting on their own view—love of one's neighbor and Christianity—and all this in front of young Nicholas, who had come into my study and broken every single thing there."

"Ah, Nicholas, do you know, I'm often troubled about little Nicholas," said Countess Mary. "He's such an unusual boy. I'm afraid I neglect him for the sake of my own children: we all have children, relations, while he has no one at all. He's always alone with his own thoughts."

"Well, I don't think you have anything to reproach yourself for on his account. Everything the fondest mother could do for her son, you have done and are doing for him, and of course I'm glad of it. He's a fine boy, a fine boy! This evening he listened to Pierre as if in a trance, and just imagine—as we were going in to supper, I looked, and he'd broken everything on my table to bits, and he told me about it himself, right away! I've never known him to tell a lie. A fine boy, a fine boy!" Nicholas repeated, though at heart he was not particularly fond of Nicholas Bolkonsky, but was always eager to acknowledge that he was a fine boy.

"Still, I'm not the same as his own mother would be," said Countess Mary. "I feel that I'm not, and it troubles me. A wonderful boy, but I'm dreadfully afraid for him. It would do him good to have some companions."

"Well, it won't be for long. Next summer I'll take him to Petersburg," said Nicholas. "Yes, Pierre always was a dreamer, and always will be," he went on, returning to the talk in the study, which had plainly unsettled him. "Well, what business is it of mine what goes on there—whether Arakcheev is bad, or any of that? What business was it of mine when I got married and was so deep in debt I was threatened with prison, and had a mother who couldn't see or understand any of it? And then there's you, and the children, and our own affairs. Do you think it's for my own pleasure that I'm out at the farm, or in the office, from morning till night? No, but I know I have to work, to comfort my mother, to repay you, and not to leave the children beggars the way I was."

Countess Mary wanted to tell him that man does not live by bread alone, and that he attached too much importance to these matters. But she knew she must not say this, and that it would be no use saying it. She only took his hand and kissed it. He took this as a sign of approval, a confirmation of his own thinking, and after a few minutes' reflection went on thinking aloud.
"You know, Mary, today Elias Mitrofanych"—this was his steward—"came back from the Tambov estate and told me they're already offering eighty thousand rubles for the forest."
And, his face eager, Nicholas began talking about the possibility of buying back Otradnoe before long, and added: "Another ten years of life, and I'll leave the children... in an excellent position."

Countess Mary listened to her husband and took in everything he told her. She knew that when he thought aloud like this, he would sometimes ask her what he had just been saying, and be annoyed if he noticed she had been thinking about something else. But she had to force herself to pay attention, because what he was saying did not interest her in the least. She looked at him, and instead of thinking, she felt something different. She felt a submissive, tender love for this man, who would never understand everything she understood, and this seemed to make her love for him even stronger, adding to it a touch of passionate tenderness. Besides this feeling, which absorbed her wholly and kept her from following the details of her husband's plans, thoughts unconnected with anything he was saying drifted through her mind. She thought of her nephew. Her husband's account of how agitated the boy had been while Pierre was speaking struck her forcibly, and various traits of his gentle, sensitive character came back to her; and thinking of her nephew, she found herself thinking of her own children too. She did not compare them with him, but compared her feeling for them with her feeling for him, and felt, with some regret, that something was lacking in her feeling for young Nicholas.

Sometimes it seemed to her that this difference came simply from the difference in their ages, but she felt herself at fault toward him, and promised herself, in her heart, to do better, to achieve the impossible—to love, in this life, her husband, her children, little Nicholas, and all her neighbors, as Christ loved mankind. Countess Mary's soul always strove toward the infinite, the eternal, the absolute, and so could never be at peace. A stern expression, marking the lofty, secret suffering of a soul weighed down by the body, showed on her face. Nicholas looked at her. "O God! What will become of us if she dies, as I always fear when her face looks like that?" he thought, and, placing himself before the icon, he began to say his evening prayers.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Natasha and Pierre, alone together, began to talk the way only a husband and wife can: with remarkable clarity and speed, each understanding and finishing the other's thoughts in ways that violated every rule of logic — no premises, no chain of reasoning, no conclusions, just their own peculiar shorthand. Natasha was so used to talking this way with her husband that for her the surest sign something was wrong between them was if Pierre started reasoning logically. When he began proving a point, arguing something out calmly and methodically, and she, following his lead, did the same, she knew they were on the edge of a quarrel.

From the moment they were alone, and Natasha came to him with her eyes wide open and happy, quickly grabbing his head and pressing it to her chest, saying, "Now you're all mine, mine! You won't get away!" — from that moment this conversation began, defying every law of logic, and defying it precisely because entirely different subjects were being discussed at the very same time. This simultaneous juggling of many topics didn't get in the way of clear understanding — on the contrary, it was the surest proof that they understood each other completely.

Just as in a dream everything is uncertain, unreasoning, and contradictory except for the feeling that steers the dream, so in this exchange — which broke every law of reason — the words themselves were not consecutive or clear, only the feeling behind them was.

Natasha talked to Pierre about her brother's life and doings, about how she'd missed being fully alive during his absence, about how she'd grown fonder than ever of Mary, and how Mary was better than her in every way. In saying this Natasha meant it sincerely — she really did believe in Mary's superiority — but at the same time, by saying it, she was making a demand on Pierre: that he should still, after all, prefer her to Mary and to every other woman, and that now, especially after seeing so many women in Petersburg, he should say so again.
Pierre, responding to Natasha's words, told her how unbearable he'd found it to meet ladies at dinners and balls in Petersburg.
"I've completely lost the knack of talking to ladies," he said. "It was simply dull. Besides, I was very busy."
Natasha looked at him intently and went on.
"Mary is wonderful," she said. "The way she understands children! It's as if she sees straight into their souls. Yesterday, for instance, Mitya was being naughty..."
"How like his father," Pierre put in.

Natasha knew exactly why he'd brought up Mitya's resemblance to Nicholas: the memory of his argument with his brother-in-law was unpleasant to him, and he wanted to know what Natasha thought about it.
"Nicholas has this weakness — he can never agree with anything that isn't generally accepted. But I understand you value what breaks new ground," she said, repeating words Pierre had once used.

"No, the main thing is that for Nicholas, ideas and arguments are a kind of amusement — almost a pastime," said Pierre. "For instance, he's building a library, and he's made it a rule never to buy a new book until he's finished the one he already has — Sismondi and Rousseau and Montesquieu," he added with a smile. "You know how much I..." he began to soften what he'd said, but Natasha cut him off to show it wasn't necessary.
"So you're saying ideas are just an amusement to him..."
"Yes, and for me nothing else is serious. The whole time I was in Petersburg I saw everyone as if in a dream. When I'm gripped by a thought, everything else is mere amusement."
"Oh, I'm so sorry I wasn't there when you met the children," said Natasha. "Which one was most excited? Lisa, I'm sure."

"Yes," Pierre replied, and went on with what was on his mind. "Nicholas says we shouldn't think so much. But I can't help it. Besides, when I was in Petersburg I felt — I can say this to you — that the whole undertaking would fall apart without me, that everyone was pulling in his own direction. But I managed to bring them all together, and my idea is so clear and so simple. You see, I'm not saying we should oppose this or that. We could be wrong. What I say is: 'Join hands, all of you who love what is right, and let there be a single banner — that of active virtue.' Prince Sergei is a fine man, and clever."

Natasha would have had no doubt at all about the greatness of Pierre's idea, except that one thing unsettled her. Can a man so important, so necessary to society, also be her husband? How did that happen? She wanted to put this doubt to him. Now who could really say whether he was cleverer than everyone else? she asked herself, and ran through everyone Pierre most respected. Judging by what he'd said, there was no one he respected as highly as Platon Karataev.
"Do you know what I'm thinking about?" she asked. "About Platon Karataev. Would he approve of you now, do you think?"
Pierre wasn't at all surprised by the question. He understood the way his wife's mind worked.
"Platon Karataev?" he repeated, and thought about it, genuinely trying to imagine what Karataev's opinion would be. "He wouldn't have understood... and yet maybe he would."
"I love you so much!" Natasha suddenly said. "So much, so much!"

"No, he wouldn't have approved," Pierre said after a pause. "What he would have approved of is our family life. He was always so eager to find decency, happiness, and peace in everything, and I would have been proud to have him see us. You know, you talk about my being away, but you wouldn't believe what a strange feeling I have for you after a separation..."
"Yes, I imagine..." Natasha began.
"No, it's not that. I never stop loving you. And it's not that I could love you more — but this is something else... Yes, of course—" he didn't finish, because their eyes meeting said the rest.

"What nonsense it is," Natasha suddenly burst out, "all that talk about honeymoons, and how the greatest happiness comes at the very beginning! It's the opposite — now is the best of all. If only you didn't have to go away! Do you remember how we used to quarrel? And it was always my fault. Always mine. And what did we even quarrel about — I don't even remember!"
"Always about the same thing," said Pierre with a smile. "Jealo—"
"Don't say it! I can't bear it!" Natasha cried, and her eyes flashed cold and fierce. "Did you see her?" she added after a pause.
"No, and if I had, I wouldn't have recognized her."
They were silent for a while.

"Oh, do you know? While you were talking in the study I was watching you," Natasha began, clearly wanting to clear away the cloud that had settled over them. "You're as alike as two peas — like the boy." (She meant their little son.) "Oh, it's time to go to him... the milk's come... but I hate to leave you."

They were both silent for a few seconds. Then suddenly, at the same moment, they both started to speak. Pierre began with self-satisfaction and enthusiasm, Natasha with a quiet, happy smile. Having interrupted each other, they both stopped to let the other go on.
"No. What were you saying? Go on, go on."
"No, you go on, I was just talking nonsense," said Natasha.

Pierre finished what he'd started to say. It was the continuation of his self-satisfied reflections on his success in Petersburg. At that moment it seemed to him that he'd been chosen to give a new direction to the whole of Russian society, and to the whole world.

"I only wanted to say that ideas with great consequences are always simple ones. My whole idea is this: if wicked people band together and become a power, then honest people must do the same. It's really as simple as that."
"Yes."
"And what were you going to say?"
"Me? Just nonsense."
"But still?"

"Oh, it's nothing, just a trifle," said Natasha, smiling more brightly still. "I only wanted to tell you about Petya: today nurse came to take him from me, and he laughed, shut his eyes, and clung to me. I'm sure he thought he was hiding. So sweet! There, now he's crying. Well, goodbye!" — and she left the room.

Meanwhile downstairs, in little Nicholas Bolkonsky's bedroom, a small lamp burned as it always did. (The boy was afraid of the dark, and they hadn't been able to cure him of it.) Dessalles slept propped up on four pillows, his Roman nose giving off a steady, rhythmic snore. Little Nicholas, who had just woken up in a cold sweat, sat up in bed and stared ahead with wide-open eyes. He'd woken from a terrible dream. He'd dreamed that he and Uncle Pierre, wearing helmets like the ones pictured in his Plutarch, were leading a huge army. The army was made up of white slanting threads that filled the air like the strands of cobweb that drift about in autumn — the ones Dessalles called les fils de la Vierge. Out in front was Glory, which looked like those same threads, only thicker. He and Pierre were being carried forward, light and joyful, closer and closer to their goal. Then suddenly the threads carrying them began to go slack and tangle, and it grew hard to move. And Uncle Nicholas stood before them, stern and threatening.

"Did you do this?" he said, pointing to some broken sealing wax and pens. "I loved you, but I have orders from Arakcheev, and I will kill the first one of you who moves forward." Little Nicholas turned to look at Pierre, but Pierre was no longer there. In his place stood his father — Prince Andrew — and his father had neither shape nor form, and yet he existed, and when little Nicholas made him out he went faint with love: he felt himself powerless, limp, formless. His father caressed him and pitied him. But Uncle Nicholas kept coming nearer and nearer to them. Terror seized young Nicholas, and he woke up.

My father! he thought. (Though there were two good portraits of Prince Andrew in the house, Nicholas never pictured him in human shape.) My father was here with me, and he caressed me. He approved of me, and of Uncle Pierre. Whatever he tells me to do, I will do. Mucius Scaevola burned his own hand. Why shouldn't something like that happen to me too? I know they want me to keep studying. And I will study. But someday I'll be finished, and then I'll do something. I only pray to God that something happens to me like what happened to Plutarch's men, and I'll act as they did. I'll do even better. Everyone will know me, love me, be delighted with me! And suddenly his chest heaved with sobs and he began to cry.
"Are you ill?" he heard Dessalles' voice ask.
"No," Nicholas answered, and lay back on his pillow.

He's good and kind, and I'm fond of him! he thought of Dessalles. But Uncle Pierre! Oh, what an extraordinary man he is! And my father? Oh, Father, Father! Yes, I will do something that even he would be satisfied with...

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 1
paragraphs: History is the life of nations and of humanity. To grasp it and put it into words — to describe directly the life of humanity, or even of a single nation — seems impossible.

The ancient historians all used one and the same method to describe and capture what seems so elusive: the life of a people. They described the actions of the individuals who ruled the people, and treated the actions of those men as standing for the actions of the whole nation.

The question — how did individual men make nations act as they wished, and what in turn guided the will of those individuals themselves? — the ancients answered by pointing to a divinity that subjected nations to the will of a chosen man, and that guided that chosen man's will toward ends already fixed in advance.
For the ancients, these questions were settled by a belief in the direct participation of God in human affairs.
Modern history, in theory, rejects both these principles.

It might seem that having rejected the ancients' belief in mankind's subjection to God, and in a predetermined goal toward which nations are led, modern history ought to study not the outward signs of power but the causes that produce it. But modern history has not done this. Having rejected the ancients' view in theory, it still follows it in practice.

Instead of men endowed with divine authority and directed straight by the will of God, modern history has given us either heroes endowed with extraordinary, superhuman gifts, or simply men of every possible kind, from monarchs down to journalists, who lead the masses. Instead of the old divinely appointed goals of the Jewish, Greek, or Roman peoples, which ancient historians took to represent the progress of humanity, modern history has set up goals of its own — the welfare of the French, the Germans, or the English, or, in its most abstract form, the welfare and civilization of humanity in general, by which is usually meant the peoples occupying a small northwestern corner of one large continent.

Modern history has rejected the beliefs of the ancients without putting a new conception in their place, and the logic of the situation has forced historians, having apparently thrown out the divine authority of kings and the "fate" of the ancients, to arrive at the very same conclusion by a different road — that is, to accept (1) that nations are guided by individual men, and (2) that there exists a known goal toward which these nations, and humanity as a whole, are moving.

At the root of the work of every modern historian from Gibbon to Buckle, despite their apparent disagreements and the seeming novelty of their outlooks, lie those same two old, unavoidable assumptions.

In the first place, the historian describes the actions of the individuals who, in his view, have directed humanity (one historian counts only monarchs, generals, and ministers as such men, while another adds orators, scholars, reformers, philosophers, and poets). Secondly, it is assumed that the goal toward which humanity is being led is known to the historians: to one of them this goal is the greatness of the Roman, Spanish, or French state; to another it is liberty, equality, and a certain kind of civilization belonging to a small corner of the world called Europe.

In 1789 a ferment breaks out in Paris; it grows, spreads, and expresses itself as a movement of peoples from west to east. Several times it surges eastward and collides with a countermovement coming from the east. In 1812 it reaches its farthest point, Moscow, and then, with remarkable symmetry, a countermovement runs from east to west, drawing in, as the first movement had, the nations of central Europe. This countermovement reaches the starting point of the first movement, in the west — Paris — and subsides.

During that twenty-year span, an immense number of fields lay untilled, houses burned down, trade shifted direction, millions of people migrated, were reduced to poverty or grew rich, and millions of Christians, who professed a law of love for their fellow men, killed one another.

What does all this mean? Why did it happen? What made these people burn houses and kill their fellow men? What were the causes of these events? What force made people act this way? These are the plain, instinctive, and entirely legitimate questions that humanity asks itself whenever it comes across the monuments and traditions of that period.
For an answer to these questions, the common sense of mankind turns to the science of history, whose purpose is to let nations and humanity come to know themselves.

If history had kept the conception held by the ancients, it would say that God, to reward or punish his people, gave Napoleon power and directed his will toward fulfilling divine ends, and that answer would be clear and complete. One might believe or disbelieve in Napoleon's divine significance, but for anyone who did believe it, nothing in the history of that period would remain unintelligible, and there would be no contradictions.
But modern history cannot give that answer. Science does not accept the ancients' notion of the direct participation of God in human affairs, and so history has to come up with other answers.
Modern history, answering these questions, says: you want to know what this movement means, what caused it, what force produced these events? Then listen:

"Louis XIV was a very proud, self-assured man; he had this mistress and that, this minister and that, and he governed France badly. His descendants were weak men, and they too governed France badly. And they had their own favorites and their own mistresses. Meanwhile certain men were writing certain books. By the end of the eighteenth century there were a couple dozen men in Paris who started talking about how all men are free and equal. This set off a wave across France in which people slashed and drowned one another. They killed the king, and a great many other people besides. At that time France had a man of genius — Napoleon. He conquered everyone everywhere, meaning he killed a great many people, because he was a great genius. And for some reason he went off to kill Africans, and killed them so thoroughly, and was so clever and cunning, that when he came home to France he ordered everyone to obey him, and everyone obeyed him. Once he had made himself Emperor, he went out again to kill people in Italy, Austria, and Prussia. And there too he killed a great many. In Russia there was an Emperor, Alexander, who decided to restore order in Europe, and so he fought against Napoleon. In 1807 the two of them suddenly became friends, but in 1811 they quarreled again and once more began killing large numbers of people. Napoleon led six hundred thousand men into Russia and captured Moscow; then he suddenly fled Moscow, and the Emperor Alexander, guided by the advice of Stein and others, united Europe to arm itself against the man who had disturbed its peace. All of Napoleon's former allies suddenly turned into his enemies, and their armies advanced against the fresh forces he had raised. The Allies defeated Napoleon, entered Paris, forced him to abdicate, and sent him to the island of Elba — without stripping him of the title of Emperor, and treating him with every mark of respect — even though five years earlier, and again a year later, they all considered him an outlaw and a brigand. Then Louis XVIII, who up to that point had been a laughingstock to both the French and the Allies, began his reign. And Napoleon, weeping in front of his Old Guard, gave up the throne and went into exile. Then the skillful statesmen and diplomats — Talleyrand above all, who managed to sit down in a particular chair before anyone else, and by doing so extended the borders of France — talked things over in Vienna, and by these conversations made whole nations happy or unhappy. Suddenly the diplomats and monarchs nearly fell out and were on the point of once again ordering their armies to kill one another, but just then Napoleon landed in France with a single battalion, and the French, who had been hating him, immediately submitted to him again, every one of them. But this enraged the Allied monarchs, and they went to fight the French once more. And they defeated the genius Napoleon and, suddenly declaring him a brigand after all, sent him off to the island of St. Helena. And the exile, cut off from the beloved France so dear to his heart, died a slow death on that rock, and left his great deeds to posterity. But in Europe a reaction set in, and the sovereigns all went back to oppressing their subjects."

It would be a mistake to think this is meant ironically — a caricature of historical writing. On the contrary, it is a fairly mild version of the contradictory answers, none of which actually meet the questions asked, given by all the historians, from the compilers of memoirs and the histories of individual states to the writers of general histories and the newest histories of the culture of that period.
The strangeness and absurdity of these answers comes from the fact that modern history, like a deaf man, answers questions nobody asked.

If the purpose of history is to describe the movement of humanity and of peoples, the first question — without an answer to which everything else remains incomprehensible — is: what is the force that moves peoples? To this, modern history laboriously answers either that Napoleon was a great genius, or that Louis XIV was very proud, or that certain writers wrote certain books.

All of that may well be true, and mankind is ready to agree with it, but it is not what was asked. All of it would be interesting if we accepted a divine power, grounded in itself, consistently steering its nations through the likes of Napoleons, Louis-es, and writers; but we do not accept such a power, and therefore, before talking about Napoleons, Louis-es, and authors, we need to be shown the connection between these men and the movement of the nations.
If some other force has taken the place of divine power, it needs to be explained what this new force actually consists of, because the whole interest of history lies precisely there.

History seems to take it for granted that this force is self-evident and known to everyone. But however much one might wish to treat it as known, anyone who reads a good number of historical works cannot help wondering whether this new force — understood so differently by the historians themselves — is really well understood by anybody at all.

chapters.title: Second Epilogue — Chapter 3
